Complete guide on working with the StatsBomb Open Data dataset (w/ applications)

Applications in Data Analytics, Network Science, Bayesian Statistics and Machine Learning.

Lucas Carrasquilla
93 min read
·
Dec 28, 2025

1. Introduction

Football analytics used to mean counts, averages, and maybe a regression if you were feeling ambitious. However, as researchers, largely out the the UK, have become more interested in the topic over the past decade, football has become one of the nicer playgrounds for applied math. We now have sophisticated techniques, informed by work in graph theory and network science, machine learning, and statistics. But you can’t do much with those tools if you don’t have a representation of the game that is precise enough to support them. That representation, in modern football analytics, is event data.

The StatsBomb Open Data repository provides a public release of high granularity event data with a schema closely aligned to professional workflows. Beyond its role as an accessible dataset, it is valuable because it allows for a concrete interface between theory and implementation. In this article, I will show you how to: (i) get and organize the data, (ii) understand the ecosystem and file architecture, (iii) load and normalize the nested JSON into tables, (iv) retrieve specific matches using identifiers, and then (v) build a practical analytics toolkit with professional visualizations (w/ MPL Soccer), passing networks and graph metrics, baseline shot/possession/defensive summaries, Bayesian estimation patterns for uncertainty-aware ratings, time-evolution analyses, and a few machine-learning workflows.

This is 2+ years of learning packed into a single article, so it’s a long read. I’ve labeled the sections with large headers so you can skip around easily. I hope it’s useful, and I’d genuinely appreciate any feedback.

The dataset is available on GitHub.

1.1 The mathematical formalization of football & StatsBomb’s role

Football looks simple until you try to model it.

The game is continuous in time, but decisions are discrete. Space matters, but space is used strategically, which means you can’t treat locations like i.i.d. points. And almost everything is multi-agent. The value of an action depends on who else is moving, where they are, and what states they can realistically reach. Historically, that complexity pushed analysts toward summary statistics such as goals, shots, possession, maybe a simple regression, etc. The problem is that those summaries are too compressed to support most of the math we’d actually like to use.

Event data changes the representation. Instead of treating a match as a single row in a dataset, you treat it as an ordered sequence of actions:

match = [e1, e2, ..., en]

each event ei comes with: timestamp, location, type, and a structured set of contextual fields.

At that point, a lot of “football questions” become standard objects:

— a possession becomes a subsequence of events,

— a passing network becomes a graph extracted from passes,

— shot quality becomes a conditional model on the state right before the shot,

— pressing becomes a spatiotemporal pattern of defensive events relative to ball location and turnovers.

StatsBomb Open Data is one of the cleanest public entry points into this view of football, because the schema is close to what you’d see in professional workflows, and the JSON structure keeps the full context, rather than flattening everything into a single table. And their open data releases were a real breakthrough in this field. By publishing event-level matches in a public repository, they made it possible to do the thing that does the most for methodological progress: implement ideas, share code, and let other people rerun it.

The repository has also expanded over time through additional public releases (World Cups, Euros, league seasons, etc.). I’m avoiding hard “as-of-today” counts here because the repo changes, but to give you a sense of scale: public writeups have described it as 3,000+ matches in recent years.

1.2 Framework

This guide is practical, but it’s also built around a simple idea: once the match is a structured event sequence, you can plug it into well-developed mathematical theory. I’d like to talk about:

Graph theory and network analysis. A team’s passing structure can be represented as a directed graph G = (V, E) , where the set of nodes V represents players, and the set of edges E represents passes.

Then you have a whole toolbox. You can use degree and weighted degree, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, PageRank measures, community detection if you want to see substructures, etc.

Bayesian statistical methods. Sports is often noisy, sample sizes are often small, and priors are often legitimate information rather than bias.

Bayesian framing is useful here because it makes uncertainty explicit and lets you stabilize estimates when the data is thin. If you want a one-line summary, it’s: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior .

You can use this for finishing rates, defensive action rates, player involvement, and even latent team strength models. Basically anywhere you’d otherwise be tempted to overinterpret small samples.

Spatial-temporal analysis. Event data is spatial by construction. In StatsBomb’s coordinate system, locations live on a standardized pitch with x running from 0 → 120 and y from 0 → 80.

That single detail matters a lot because it defines everything you do next: binning into zones, measuring progression, building threat models, defining “the box”, computing angles, and building state representations for ML models.

Machine learning applications. Once you’ve built reliable tables from the JSON, you can do the standard ML loop: feature construction, then labeling , then training, then evaluation, but with two football-specific constraints:

  1. your features are usually structured context (location, pressure, body part, pass height, defensive density, etc.), and
  2. leakage is easy if you don’t define the prediction moment carefully (e.g., using information that only exists after the action).

In this article I’ll keep the ML pieces grounded. Clustering for style, classification for event outcomes, and predictive models for things like shot quality and possession value.

1.3 Things you should know

Before we begin, I’d like to state that this guide is written for readers who have some background in the topics we’ll be using. You do not need to be an expert in any of these, I know I’m not, but you should recognize the objects and be able to follow definitions.

You should be familiar with:

— Linear Algebra: Vectors and matrices, basic linear maps, eigenvectors and eigenvalues at a conceptual level. This shows up when we build passing networks, compute centrality measures, and do dimensionality-reduction methods such as PCA.

— Probability: Random variables, conditional probability, and obviously Bayes’ Theorem. You need to be able to read statements like “estimate P(outcome | context)” and understand what’s being said.

— Statistics: Estimation and uncertainty. In practice: regression, maximum likelihood, and what a confidence interval is saying.

— Graph Theory: Nodes, edges, paths, directed vs undirected graphs, weighted edges. Enough to interpret a pass network as a graph and compute simple structural summaries.

— Programming: Python fluency with the standard scientific computing libraries: numpy ,pandas, and plotting (I’ll use matplotlib, and mplsoccer later for pitch plots) is useful. If you’re comfortable reading JSON and writing functions, you’re fine.

With that said, let’s begin.

2. Understanding the StatsBomb Open Data dataset’s structure

In this section, we will examine the dataset’s hierarchical organization, quantify its scope and coverage, and establish the mathematical framework for subsequent analyses. Through some exploration of the data architecture, we can identify key statistical properties and structural characteristics that inform our approach.

2.1 Dataset overview

StatsBomb Open Data is organized around a simple indexing chain:

  • competitions.json lists competition–season entries (this is the first place you get IDs).
  • Matches live under data/matches/{competition_id}/{season_id}.json.
  • Events and lineups live under data/events/{match_id}.json and data/lineups/{match_id}.json.
  • For some matches, 360 context lives under data/three-sixty/{match_id}.json.

So when we talk about “how big the dataset is,” we usually mean four different things:

  1. Number of entries in competitions.json (competition–season pairs),
  2. number of unique competitions,
  3. number of matches available across those entries,
  4. number of events per match (which varies a lot).

The important principle is this: don’t freeze these into constants. The repo changes. Instead, compute them from the files you pulled, and report them as in your local copy.

Here’s a baseline function that loads competitions.json and prints a reproducible summary:

import json
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

def load_competitions(repo_root: str | Path) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict]:
    """
    Load StatsBomb Open Data competitions.json and return:
      (1) competitions dataframe
      (2) a small summary dict you can print or log

    Parameters
    ----------
    repo_root : str | Path
        Path to the *root* of the statsbomb/open-data repository clone.

    Returns
    -------
    competitions_df : pd.DataFrame
    summary : dict
    """
    repo_root = Path(repo_root)
    comp_path = repo_root / "data" / "competitions.json"

    if not comp_path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Could not find {comp_path}. "
            "Make sure repo_root points to the cloned statsbomb/open-data directory."
        )

    competitions_data = json.loads(comp_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    competitions_df = pd.DataFrame(competitions_data)

    # These column names are stable in the open-data schema (gender was added in v1.1). :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
    summary = {
        "entries_competitions_json": len(competitions_df),  # competition-season entries
        "unique_competitions": competitions_df["competition_name"].nunique(),
        "unique_seasons": competitions_df["season_name"].nunique(),
        "countries": competitions_df["country_name"].nunique(),
        "genders": competitions_df["competition_gender"].value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict(),
    }

    return competitions_df, summary


# Example usage
competitions_df, summary = load_competitions(r"/path/to/statsbomb/open-data")

print("=== DATASET SCOPE (local copy) ===")
for k, v in summary.items():
    print(f"{k}: {v}")

# Quick look at what fields you have
print("\nColumns:", sorted(competitions_df.columns))
print("\nSample rows:")
print(competitions_df.head(3))

At the metadata level, StatsBomb Open Data follows a hierarchical structure. A competition has seasons; a season has matches; a match has event files (and sometimes 360 files). If you want a formal picture, you can think of the repository as a directed tree where edges point downstream:

Competition
└── Season
    └── Match
        ├── events
        ├── lineups
        └── 360 (sometimes)

Below is a hierarchy summary. It answers: which competitions have the most seasons in your local copy, and how concentrated is coverage across competitions?

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def analyze_competition_hierarchy(competitions_df: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """
    Summarize the competition→season hierarchy encoded in competitions.json.

    Returns a dict so you can log it, print it, or reuse it in later sections.
    """
    comp_counts = competitions_df["competition_name"].value_counts()

    seasons_per_comp = comp_counts.to_numpy()

    summary = {
        "top_competitions_by_seasons": comp_counts.head(10),
        "seasons_per_competition": {
            "mean": float(np.mean(seasons_per_comp)),
            "median": float(np.median(seasons_per_comp)),
            "std": float(np.std(seasons_per_comp, ddof=0)),
            "min": int(np.min(seasons_per_comp)),
            "max": int(np.max(seasons_per_comp)),
        }
    }

    print("=== COMPETITION HIERARCHY (local copy) ===")
    print("Top competitions by number of seasons available:")
    for comp, n in summary["top_competitions_by_seasons"].items():
        print(f"  {comp}: {n}")

    stats = summary["seasons_per_competition"]
    print("\nSeasons per competition (distribution summary):")
    print(f"  mean={stats['mean']:.2f} | median={stats['median']:.2f} | std={stats['std']:.2f} | min={stats['min']} | max={stats['max']}")

    return summary

hierarchy_summary = analyze_competition_hierarchy(competitions_df)

Some matches include StatsBomb 360: which is freeze-frame context around events, like who is on the pitch at the moment of an action, and where. This is qualitatively different from simple event data because it exposes higher-dimensional context, exactly the stuff most event-only models are trying to approximate.

In the open-data repo, 360 availability is indicated in the competition metadata (and then realized as separate files under data/three-sixty/). In practice you want to answer one key question: which competition–season entries have 360 availability?

Here’s a function that does that:

def analyze_360_coverage(competitions_df):
    """
    Analyze StatsBomb 360 data availability and coverage patterns.
    
    Returns:
    dict: 360 data coverage statistics and patterns
    """
    # Identify competitions with 360 data
    has_360 = competitions_df[competitions_df['match_available_360'].notna()]
    
    print("=== STATSBOMB 360 DATA COVERAGE ===")
    print(f"Competitions with 360 data: {len(has_360)} / {len(competitions_df)} ({100*len(has_360)/len(competitions_df):.1f}%)")
    
    if len(has_360) > 0:
        print("\nCompetitions with 360 data:")
        for _, row in has_360.iterrows():
            print(f"  {row['competition_name']} {row['season_name']}")
        
        # Temporal analysis of 360 data availability
        has_360['year'] = has_360['season_name'].str.extract('(\d{4})', expand=False).astype(float)
        year_analysis = has_360.groupby('year').size()
        
        print(f"\n360 Data Temporal Distribution:")
        for year, count in year_analysis.items():
            if not np.isnan(year):
                print(f"  {int(year)}: {count} competitions")
    
    return {
        'total_360_competitions': len(has_360),
        'coverage_percentage': 100 * len(has_360) / len(competitions_df),
        '360_competitions': has_360[['competition_name', 'season_name', 'match_available_360']]
    }

coverage_360 = analyze_360_coverage(competitions)

Event data tells you what happened and where, but 360 data gives you a snapshot of what the pitch looked like at that instant.

2.2 Dataset structure

As I’ve established, the StatsBomb Open Data repository is easiest to understand as a hierarchy: metadata at the top, match lists in the middle, and match-specific files at the bottom. Conceptually, you can think of the directory layout as a tree T = (V, E) where nodes represent “levels” (competitions, seasons, matches, events) and edges represent containment. The benefit of thinking this way is that it tells you exactly where identifiers are introduced, and exactly which identifiers you need to traverse the dataset without guessing filenames:

├── data/
│   ├── competitions.json          # Competition metadata (|C| entries)
│   ├── matches/                   # Match-level data
│   │   └── {competition_id}/
│   │       └── {season_id}.json   # Matches for specific competition-season
│   ├── events/                    # Event-level data
│   │   └── {match_id}.json        # Events for specific match
│   ├── lineups/                   # Player lineup data
│   │   └── {match_id}.json        # Lineups for specific match
│   └── three-sixty/               # 360-degree tracking data
│       └── {match_id}.json        # 360 data for specific match
├── doc/                           # Technical documentation
└── img/

A few points are worth making explicit:

— competitions.json is the global index. It does not contain matches or events; it tells you which competition–season entries exist and gives you the IDs you’ll need later.

— Match lists are stored by (competition_id, season_id), not by competition name.

— Event data is stored by match_id. That means your workflow should always flow IDs → file paths, never names → file paths.

The function below is a quick check for your local clone:

def analyze_data_structure(data_path):
    """
    Analyze the file structure and organizational hierarchy of StatsBomb data.
    
    Parameters:
    data_path (str): Path to StatsBomb data directory
    
    Returns:
    dict: Structural analysis with file counts and organization metrics
    """
    from pathlib import Path
    
    data_dir = Path(data_path) / "data"
    
    # Analyze directory structure
    structure_analysis = {
        'competitions_file': (data_dir / "competitions.json").exists(),
        'events_dir': (data_dir / "events").exists(),
        'matches_dir': (data_dir / "matches").exists(),
        'lineups_dir': (data_dir / "lineups").exists(),
        'three_sixty_dir': (data_dir / "three-sixty").exists()
    }
    
    print("=== DATA STRUCTURE VALIDATION ===")
    for component, exists in structure_analysis.items():
        status = "✓" if exists else "✗"
        print(f"{status} {component.replace('_', ' ').title()}: {'Found' if exists else 'Missing'}")
    
    # Count files in each directory
    if structure_analysis['events_dir']:
        events_count = len(list((data_dir / "events").glob("*.json")))
        print(f"\nFile Counts:")
        print(f"  Event files: {events_count}")
        
        if structure_analysis['lineups_dir']:
            lineups_count = len(list((data_dir / "lineups").glob("*.json")))
            print(f"  Lineup files: {lineups_count}")
            
        if structure_analysis['three_sixty_dir']:
            three_sixty_count = len(list((data_dir / "three-sixty").glob("*.json")))
            print(f"  360 tracking files: {three_sixty_count}")
    
    return structure_analysis

structure_validation = analyze_data_structure("path/to/statsbomb/data")

StatsBomb data is JSON based, which means the schema is not flat. Fields such as teams, players and event types appear as nested objects (dictionaries), and some attributes only exist for particular event types. This actually determines how you should parse and validate the data, and it’s the reason many “quick” pipelines will often introduce errors.

At the match level, the JSON objects act like structured metadata containers: you get match identifiers, date/time fields, competition and season context, and nested team objects. The goal here is not to memorize every field, but to understand the shape of the object you’ll be joining against later.

The code below loads a single competition–season match list and prints a summary, plus a single match example to show the nested structure:

def analyze_match_structure(data_path, competition_id=11, season_id=90):
    """
    Analyze match-level data structure for a specific competition-season pair.
    
    Parameters:
    data_path (str): Path to StatsBomb data
    competition_id (int): Competition identifier
    season_id (int): Season identifier
    
    Returns:
    dict: Match structure analysis with schema information
    """
    matches_path = Path(data_path) / "data" / "matches" / str(competition_id) / f"{season_id}.json"
    
    if not matches_path.exists():
        return {"error": f"Matches file not found: {matches_path}"}
    
    with open(matches_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        matches_data = json.load(f)
    
    matches_df = pd.DataFrame(matches_data)
    
    print("=== MATCH STRUCTURE ANALYSIS ===")
    print(f"Competition ID: {competition_id}, Season ID: {season_id}")
    print(f"Total matches: {len(matches_df)}")
    print(f"Schema columns: {list(matches_df.columns)}")
    
    # Analyze match metadata
    if len(matches_df) > 0:
        sample_match = matches_df.iloc[0]
        print(f"\nSample Match Metadata:")
        print(f"  Match ID: {sample_match.get('match_id')}")
        print(f"  Date: {sample_match.get('match_date')}")
        print(f"  Kick-off: {sample_match.get('kick_off')}")
        
        # Extract team information
        home_team = sample_match.get('home_team', {})
        away_team = sample_match.get('away_team', {})
        print(f"  Home team: {home_team.get('home_team_name', 'Unknown')}")
        print(f"  Away team: {away_team.get('away_team_name', 'Unknown')}")
        
        # Temporal analysis
        if 'match_date' in matches_df.columns:
            dates = pd.to_datetime(matches_df['match_date'])
            print(f"\nTemporal Coverage:")
            print(f"  Date range: {dates.min().date()} to {dates.max().date()}")
            print(f"  Duration: {(dates.max() - dates.min()).days} days")
    
    return {
        "matches_df": matches_df,
        "total_matches": len(matches_df),
        "schema_columns": list(matches_df.columns)
    }
# Example: Analyze La Liga 2020/21 season
match_structure = analyze_match_structure("path/to/data", competition_id=11, season_id=90)

if you plan to analyze events, you should treat the match file as your the “spine” of your joins. Almost everything you care about later (teams, match date, competition context, score, etc.) is either here or indexed from here.

2.3 Data quality

Event files are the core of the dataset. Each match corresponds to a single event log, which is a time-ordered sequence of actions with structured attributes. It is helpful to describe this as a sequence E_m = [e1, e2, …, e_{n_m}], where n_m is the number of recorded events in match m.

Two things are very relevant:

  1. granularity (how much is recorded), and
  2. heterogeneity (how event structure changes by event type).

This function below will tell you how many events exist, how many event types appear, which types dominate, and how much spatial information is present:

def analyze_event_structure(data_path, match_id):
    """
    Detailed analysis of event data structure and mathematical properties.
    
    Parameters:
    data_path (str): Path to StatsBomb data
    match_id (int): Specific match identifier
    
    Returns:
    dict: Comprehensive event structure analysis
    """
    events_path = Path(data_path) / "data" / "events" / f"{match_id}.json"
    
    if not events_path.exists():
        return {"error": f"Events file not found for match {match_id}"}
    
    with open(events_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        events_data = json.load(f)
    
    events_df = pd.DataFrame(events_data)
    
    print("=== EVENT DATA STRUCTURE ANALYSIS ===")
    print(f"Match ID: {match_id}")
    print(f"Total events: {len(events_df)} = n_m")
    print(f"Event schema dimensions: {events_df.shape}")
    print(f"Column count: {len(events_df.columns)}")
    
    # Event type distribution analysis
    if 'type' in events_df.columns:
        event_types = events_df['type'].apply(
            lambda x: x['name'] if isinstance(x, dict) else str(x)
        ).value_counts()
        
        print(f"\nEvent Type Distribution (|E_type|):")
        print(f"Unique event types: {len(event_types)}")
        
        # Top 10 most frequent events
        for event_type, count in event_types.head(10).items():
            percentage = (count / len(events_df)) * 100
            print(f"  {event_type}: {count} ({percentage:.1f}%)")
        
        # Statistical analysis of event frequencies
        frequencies = event_types.values
        print(f"\nFrequency Statistics:")
        print(f"  Mean events per type: {np.mean(frequencies):.1f}")
        print(f"  Median events per type: {np.median(frequencies):.1f}")
        print(f"  Standard deviation: {np.std(frequencies):.1f}")
    
    # Spatial data availability analysis
    spatial_events = events_df[events_df['location'].notna()]
    spatial_coverage = len(spatial_events) / len(events_df) * 100
    
    print(f"\nSpatial Data Coverage:")
    print(f"  Events with location: {len(spatial_events)} / {len(events_df)} ({spatial_coverage:.1f}%)")
    
    # Temporal structure analysis
    if 'minute' in events_df.columns and 'second' in events_df.columns:
        temporal_analysis = {
            'min_minute': events_df['minute'].min(),
            'max_minute': events_df['minute'].max(),
            'periods': events_df['period'].nunique() if 'period' in events_df.columns else 'Unknown'
        }
        
        print(f"\nTemporal Structure:")
        print(f"  Time range: {temporal_analysis['min_minute']}' to {temporal_analysis['max_minute']}'")
        print(f"  Periods: {temporal_analysis['periods']}")
    
    return {
        "events_df": events_df,
        "total_events": len(events_df),
        "event_types": event_types if 'type' in events_df.columns else {},
        "spatial_coverage": spatial_coverage,
        "schema_columns": list(events_df.columns)
    }

In most matches, a small number of event types accounts for the majority of rows (passes, ball receipts, carries, pressures, etc.), and many event types are rare. This “long tail” shows up later when you build models: it’s where sparsity and unstable estimates will come from.

2.3.1 Coordinate system

StatsBomb’s event locations are recorded in a standardized pitch coordinate system with dimensions 120 × 80 (in dataset units). That standardization is what makes it possible to compare shot maps across matches, build zone-based summaries, and compute geometry-driven features (angles, distances, progression, etc.).

But before you do any of that, you want to validate two basics:

  1. Are locations present for the event types you’re using?

2. Do coordinates actually fall inside the expected bounds?

The function below does that:

def analyze_coordinate_system(events_df):
    """
    Analyze the StatsBomb coordinate system and spatial data properties.
    
    Parameters:
    events_df (pd.DataFrame): Events data with location information
    
    Returns:
    dict: Spatial coordinate analysis with mathematical properties
    """
    # Extract location data
    locations = []
    for _, event in events_df.iterrows():
        location = event.get('location')
        if location and isinstance(location, list) and len(location) >= 2:
            locations.append([location[0], location[1]])
    
    if not locations:
        return {"error": "No valid location data found"}
    
    locations_array = np.array(locations)
    x_coords = locations_array[:, 0]
    y_coords = locations_array[:, 1]
    
    print("=== COORDINATE SYSTEM ANALYSIS ===")
    print("Pitch Dimensions: 120 × 80 units")
    
    # Statistical analysis of coordinates
    print(f"\nX-Coordinate Statistics:")
    print(f"  Range: [{np.min(x_coords):.1f}, {np.max(x_coords):.1f}]")
    print(f"  Mean: {np.mean(x_coords):.1f}")
    print(f"  Standard deviation: {np.std(x_coords):.1f}")
    
    print(f"\nY-Coordinate Statistics:")
    print(f"  Range: [{np.min(y_coords):.1f}, {np.max(y_coords):.1f}]")
    print(f"  Mean: {np.mean(y_coords):.1f}")
    print(f"  Standard deviation: {np.std(y_coords):.1f}")
    
    # Boundary validation
    x_valid = np.all((x_coords >= 0) & (x_coords <= 120))
    y_valid = np.all((y_coords >= 0) & (y_coords <= 80))
    
    print(f"\nBoundary Validation:")
    print(f"  X-coordinates within [0, 120]: {x_valid}")
    print(f"  Y-coordinates within [0, 80]: {y_valid}")
    
    # Spatial density analysis
    pitch_area = 120 * 80  # Total pitch area
    events_per_unit = len(locations) / pitch_area
    
    print(f"\nSpatial Density:")
    print(f"  Total events with location: {len(locations)}")
    print(f"  Events per unit area: {events_per_unit:.4f}")
    
    return {
        "total_locations": len(locations),
        "x_stats": {"min": np.min(x_coords), "max": np.max(x_coords), 
                   "mean": np.mean(x_coords), "std": np.std(x_coords)},
        "y_stats": {"min": np.min(y_coords), "max": np.max(y_coords), 
                   "mean": np.mean(y_coords), "std": np.std(y_coords)},
        "boundary_valid": x_valid and y_valid,
        "spatial_density": events_per_unit
    }

2.3.2 Missing values

Missingness is often times part of the data-generating process. Some columns are structurally missing because they only apply to certain event types, and some fields are missing because context is genuinely unavailable or undefined for a given action.

So the goal here is not “drop rows with nulls.” The goal is to characterize missingness, identify which fields are relevant for your workflow, and build habits that prevent accidental filtering.

This function below provides a completeness summary with: overall missingness, the columns with the most missing values, critical-field completeness, and location completeness as a special case:

def analyze_data_completeness(events_df):
    """
    Analysis of data completeness and missing value patterns.
    
    Parameters:
    events_df (pd.DataFrame): Events data for completeness analysis
    
    Returns:
    dict: Missing data analysis with mathematical characterization
    """
    print("=== DATA COMPLETENESS ANALYSIS ===")
    
    # Overall completeness
    total_cells = events_df.size
    missing_cells = events_df.isnull().sum().sum()
    completeness = (total_cells - missing_cells) / total_cells * 100
    
    print(f"Overall Data Completeness: {completeness:.2f}%")
    print(f"Total data points: {total_cells:,}")
    print(f"Missing data points: {missing_cells:,}")
    
    # Column-wise missingness analysis
    missing_by_column = events_df.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
    non_zero_missing = missing_by_column[missing_by_column > 0]
    
    if len(non_zero_missing) > 0:
        print(f"\nColumns with Missing Data:")
        for column, missing_count in non_zero_missing.head(10).items():
            missing_percentage = (missing_count / len(events_df)) * 100
            print(f"  {column}: {missing_count} ({missing_percentage:.1f}%)")
    else:
        print(f"\nNo missing data detected in primary columns.")
    
    # Critical field completeness
    critical_fields = ['id', 'minute', 'second', 'type', 'team']
    critical_completeness = {}
    
    print(f"\nCritical Field Completeness:")
    for field in critical_fields:
        if field in events_df.columns:
            missing = events_df[field].isnull().sum()
            completeness = (len(events_df) - missing) / len(events_df) * 100
            critical_completeness[field] = completeness
            print(f"  {field}: {completeness:.1f}% complete")
    
    # Spatial data completeness patterns
    location_missing = events_df['location'].isnull().sum() if 'location' in events_df.columns else len(events_df)
    location_completeness = (len(events_df) - location_missing) / len(events_df) * 100
    
    print(f"\nSpatial Data Completeness:")
    print(f"  Location data: {location_completeness:.1f}% complete")
    
    return {
        "overall_completeness": completeness,
        "missing_by_column": missing_by_column.to_dict(),
        "critical_completeness": critical_completeness,
        "spatial_completeness": location_completeness
    }

In any application, you should always completeness reports as part of your pipeline output. If a later change in parsing suddenly shifts location completeness from, say, 90% to 30%, you want to catch that immediately before you trust any model or visualization.

2.4 Statistical properties of the dataset

Once you load a match or a whole competition into an event table, the first mathematical object you meet is the frequency distribution over event types. This distribution will dictate:

— what “typical” means in the data,

— -whether asymptotics are trustworthy,

— how severe class imbalance will be in ML,

— and whether a model should treat counts as roughly Poisson-like noise or as something far more heavy-tailed.

In most event datasets, event-type frequencies are strongly unequal. A small set of event types accounts for a large share of all events (passes and receipts dominate), while many event types are rare. That pattern is a long-tail distribution, and it changes how you should reason about inference.

Below is a diagnostics block that will tell you how to measure that inequality and tail behavior in a few complementary ways:

  1. Mean / median / standard deviation of type frequencies.

These are the first sanity checks. The key comparison is mean vs median:

  • if mean >> median, the distribution is dominated by a few very frequent event types.
  • a large standard deviation relative to the mean indicates strong dispersion and heterogeneity across types.

2. Skewness.

Skewness measures asymmetry. For event-type frequencies you should expect positive skewness: many small counts and a few huge ones.

Numerically:

  • skewness near 0 suggests symmetry (rare here),
  • large positive values indicate a heavy right tail.

3. Kurtosis.

In pandas, kurtosis() is typically “excess kurtosis” (normal distribution ≈ 0). Interpretations:

  • > 0 means heavier tails / more outlier-prone than a Gaussian baseline.
  • Very large values are exactly what long-tail frequency data produces: a handful of event types behave like outliers relative to the bulk.

4. Log–log correlation between rank and frequency.

If you sort event types by frequency and look at log(rank) vs log(frequency), a roughly linear relationship suggests a Zipf-like regime: frequency ≈ k * rank^{-α} over some range.

You should compute the correlation coefficient between those two log sequences:

  • a value close to -1 means “very linear and decreasing” in log–log space (strong Zipf-like signature),
  • closer to 0 means no clear scaling pattern,
  • positive would be structurally very weird here.

5. Gini coefficient of event-type frequencies.

This is the cleanest single-number summary of inequality across types. Gini = 0 means all event types occur equally often; Gini = 1 means one type accounts for essentially everything.

In event logs, you should expect a meaningfully positive Gini because the game generates certain actions (passes, receptions, carries) far more often than others (e.g., penalties, own goals, some card events, etc.). High Gini is not a data quality issue; it is a structural property of the game and the recording scheme.

6. Mean events per minute.

This standard formula: len(events_df) / 90 is an intensity estimate under a simplifying assumption of exactly 90 minutes. It’s a useful baseline, but interpret it as approximate, because:

  • matches include added time,
  • some competitions include more stoppages,
  • and minute is a coarse discretization (real timestamps carry more granularity).

7. Peak minute.

The most common minute can be meaningful (bursts in stoppage time), but it can also reflect discretization artifacts: events near boundaries (45, 90) can pile up because “minute” bins many distinct seconds into the same integer. If you see spikes at 45/90, that often says more about binning than football.

8. Variance of minute.

This is a bounded variance because minute ∈ [0, 90]. A useful comparison is the discrete-uniform baseline: if events were spread uniformly across minutes 0..90, the variance would be approximately
Var_uniform ≈ (91^2 - 1)/12 ≈ 690.

So:

  • variance much smaller than ~690 implies concentration toward the middle of the interval (or toward particular phases),
  • variance closer to ~690 suggests a relatively even spread,
  • variance patterns across matches can reveal tempo differences, stoppage concentration, or simply recording density differences.

Here is a function to get all of these:

def analyze_statistical_properties(events_df):
    """
    Analyze statistical properties and mathematical characteristics of event data.
    
    Parameters:
    events_df (pd.DataFrame): Events data for statistical analysis
    
    Returns:
    dict: Statistical analysis with distribution characteristics
    """
    print("=== STATISTICAL PROPERTIES ANALYSIS ===")
    
    # Event type frequency distribution
    if 'type' in events_df.columns:
        event_types = events_df['type'].apply(
            lambda x: x['name'] if isinstance(x, dict) else str(x)
        ).value_counts()
        
        frequencies = event_types.values
        
        # Distribution statistics
        print(f"Event Frequency Distribution:")
        print(f"  Number of event types: {len(event_types)}")
        print(f"  Mean frequency: {np.mean(frequencies):.2f}")
        print(f"  Median frequency: {np.median(frequencies):.2f}")
        print(f"  Standard deviation: {np.std(frequencies):.2f}")
        print(f"  Skewness: {pd.Series(frequencies).skew():.2f}")
        print(f"  Kurtosis: {pd.Series(frequencies).kurtosis():.2f}")
        
        # Power law analysis
        log_ranks = np.log(np.arange(1, len(frequencies) + 1))
        log_frequencies = np.log(frequencies)
        correlation = np.corrcoef(log_ranks, log_frequencies)[0, 1]
        
        print(f"  Log-log correlation: {correlation:.3f}")
        
        # Gini coefficient for frequency inequality
        sorted_freq = np.sort(frequencies)
        n = len(sorted_freq)
        cumsum = np.cumsum(sorted_freq)
        gini = (n + 1 - 2 * np.sum(cumsum) / cumsum[-1]) / n
        
        print(f"  Gini coefficient: {gini:.3f}")
    
    # Temporal distribution analysis
    if 'minute' in events_df.columns:
        minute_dist = events_df['minute'].value_counts().sort_index()
        
        print(f"\nTemporal Distribution:")
        print(f"  Events per minute (mean): {len(events_df) / 90:.1f}")
        print(f"  Peak minute: {minute_dist.idxmax()} ({minute_dist.max()} events)")
        print(f"  Temporal variance: {events_df['minute'].var():.2f}")
    
    return {
        "event_type_stats": {
            "mean_frequency": np.mean(frequencies) if 'type' in events_df.columns else None,
            "frequency_std": np.std(frequencies) if 'type' in events_df.columns else None,
            "gini_coefficient": gini if 'type' in events_df.columns else None
        },
        "temporal_stats": {
            "mean_events_per_minute": len(events_df) / 90 if 'minute' in events_df.columns else None,
            "temporal_variance": events_df['minute'].var() if 'minute' in events_df.columns else None
        }
    }

If you see mean >> median, high positive skewness, high excess kurtosis, and a high Gini, you’re in the regime where “average event type” is not a meaningful object. Most types are rare; a few dominate.

Practical consequences:

— In ML, you need to treat type prediction as class-imbalanced (think weighting).

— In inference, rare types will have unstable estimates; shrinkage (Bayesian priors / hierarchical models) or pooling across contexts is essential because of this.

— For count modeling across types, simple Poisson assumptions often understate dispersion; you’ll often need models that tolerate overdispersion or heterogeneity.

If log–log correlation is strongly negative (close to -1), that’s a signal that rank-frequency scaling is present (at least approximately). That’s the mathematical fingerprint of “few very common actions + long tail of specialized actions,” and it is exactly why naive feature spaces explode in dimensionality.

For temporal summaries, treat minute as a coarse intensity proxy. If you care about time dynamics (tempo, transitions, pressure waves), you eventually want to move from minute to higher-resolution timestamps and/or possession-phase segmentation. But even this coarse view helps you detect anomalies quickly (a match with weird spikes, parsing issues, or unexpected distributions).

To call the function:

# Example statistical analysis
if 'events_df' in locals():
    statistical_properties = analyze_statistical_properties(events_df)

3. Data Exploration

This section provides a step-by-step tutorial for accessing and performing initial exploration of the StatsBomb Open Data repository. Through an example using La Liga 2020/21 season data, we demonstrate the complete pipeline from environment setup to some more advanced event analysis.

3.1 Setting Up Your Environment

Our analysis framework requires several Python libraries:

# Core data manipulation and mathematical computing
import pandas as pd           # DataFrame operations and data analysis
import numpy as np           # Numerical computing and linear algebra
import json                  # JSON data parsing for StatsBomb format

# Statistical analysis and visualization
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # Publication-quality plotting
import seaborn as sns           # Statistical data visualization
from pathlib import Path       # Cross-platform file system operations
from scipy import stats       # Statistical distributions and tests

Let’s begin with the root node (competitions) and traverse to leaf nodes (individual events):

def load_and_analyze_competitions(data_path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Load competition data and perform comprehensive statistical analysis.

    - Let C = {c₁, c₂, ..., cₙ} be the set of competitions
    - Each cᵢ has attributes: name, country, gender, seasons
    - We analyze |C|, geographical distribution, and temporal coverage
    """
    comp_path = Path(data_path) / "data" / "competitions.json"
    
    with open(comp_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        competitions_data = json.load(f)
    
    competitions = pd.DataFrame(competitions_data)
    
    # Statistical characterization
    print("COMPETITION DATA ANALYSIS")
    print("=" * 40)
    print(f"Total entries (|C × S|): {len(competitions)}")
    print(f"Unique competitions (|C|): {competitions['competition_name'].nunique()}")
    print(f"Geographic coverage: {competitions['country_name'].nunique()} countries")
    print(f"Temporal span: {competitions['season_name'].min()} to {competitions['season_name'].max()}")
    
    # Competition frequency distribution
    comp_counts = competitions['competition_name'].value_counts()
    print(f"\nFrequency Distribution Statistics:")
    print(f"  Mean seasons per competition: {comp_counts.mean():.2f}")
    print(f"  Standard deviation: {comp_counts.std():.2f}")
    print(f"  Coefficient of variation: {comp_counts.std()/comp_counts.mean():.3f}")
    
    return competitions

Let the dataset define a finite index set of competition–season pairs

so that each (c, s) in D induces a collection of matches and (when available) event streams. The distribution of coverage across competitions is very heterogeneous; a compact way to quantify this dispersion is the coefficient of variation

In our sample, CV = 1.429, which indicates a mixture of (i) a few competitions with multi-season longitudinal depth and (ii) many competitions with sparse, “thin slice” coverage.

Panel A (Competition Frequency): Champions League and La Liga dominate with 18 seasons each, representing 48% of total coverage. This follows a power-law distribution typical of sports data hierarchies.

Panel B (Gender Distribution): 89.3% male vs. 10.7% female competitions reflects historical data availability patterns, with growing female representation in recent years.

Panel C (Geographic Distribution): European competitions represent 76.9% of coverage, indicating geographic bias toward established football analytics markets.

Panel D (Season Distribution): The bimodal distribution suggests two distinct data collection strategies: comprehensive multi-season coverage for major competitions and single-season samples for historical analysis.

3.2 Deep dive with a concrete example

To demonstrate some more advanced analytical capabilities, let’s conduct a case study using La Liga 2020/21 (competition_id=11, season_id=90).

def analyze_laliga_2020_21(data_path: str) -> tuple:
    """
    Comprehensive analysis of La Liga 2020/21 season.
    
    Mathematical Framework:
    - Season S contains matches M = {m₁, m₂, ..., m₃₈₀}
    - Each match mᵢ has goals gᵢ = (home_goals, away_goals)
    - We analyze goal distributions, team performance, and temporal patterns
    """
    matches_path = Path(data_path) / "data" / "matches" / "11" / "90.json"
    
    with open(matches_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        matches_data = json.load(f)
    
    matches_df = pd.DataFrame(matches_data)
    
    # Extract match outcome variables
    home_scores = [match['home_score'] for match in matches_data]
    away_scores = [match['away_score'] for match in matches_data]
    total_goals = [h + a for h, a in zip(home_scores, away_scores)]
    
    # Statistical analysis
    print("LA LIGA 2020/21 STATISTICAL ANALYSIS")
    print("=" * 45)
    print(f"Sample size (n): {len(matches_df)} matches")
    print(f"Total goals: {sum(total_goals)}")
    print(f"Mean goals per match (μ): {np.mean(total_goals):.3f}")
    print(f"Standard deviation (σ): {np.std(total_goals):.3f}")
    print(f"Variance (σ²): {np.var(total_goals):.3f}")
    
    # Distributional analysis
    from scipy import stats
    
    # Test for Poisson distribution (common in football)
    lambda_est = np.mean(total_goals)
    ks_stat, p_value = stats.kstest(total_goals, 
                                   lambda x: stats.poisson.cdf(x, lambda_est))
    
    print(f"Poisson distribution test:")
    print(f"  Estimated λ: {lambda_est:.3f}")
    print(f"  KS statistic: {ks_stat:.4f}")
    print(f"  p-value: {p_value:.4f}")
    
    # Home advantage analysis
    home_wins = sum(1 for h, a in zip(home_scores, away_scores) if h > a)
    draws = sum(1 for h, a in zip(home_scores, away_scores) if h == a)
    away_wins = sum(1 for h, a in zip(home_scores, away_scores) if h < a)
    
    home_advantage = home_wins / len(matches_df)
    print(f"\nHome advantage analysis:")
    print(f"  Home win rate: {home_advantage:.3f}")
    print(f"  Expected (null hypothesis): 0.333")
    print(f"  Observed deviation: {(home_advantage - 0.333):.3f}")
    
    return matches_df, home_scores, away_scores, total_goals

Let M = {1, ..., n} index matches in the competition-season, and let G_i denote total goals in match i. The empirical mean

equals 3.37, which motivates the classical modeling baseline:

This Poisson reference point is analytically very useful because it provides (i) a canonical likelihood for goals, (ii) a variance benchmark (Var(G) = λ) for diagnosing over-dispersion, and (iii) a gateway to hierarchical extensions (team attack/defense effects; match-state effects).

Outcome shares (home/draw/away) provide an interpretable summary of competitive balance and home advantage. One can formalize “home advantage” as a deviation from the null p_home = p_away (or from a league-specific baseline). Here, the home share exceeds a naïve benchmark and is reported as statistically significant via a standard normal approximation.

Importantly, this is a statement about outcome frequencies, not mechanism. Identifying causes requires controlling for team strength and match context.

Figure 2 complements Table 2 by revealing distributional shape (not just moments): the histogram of G_i visualizes the tail probability of high-scoring matches, while the team-level goal totals highlight a pronounced concentration of scoring in a small subset of teams, suggesting that a homogeneous Poisson model is at best a first approximation and that heterogeneity is structurally present.

Another thing you can do is calculate a performance vector for each team:

def calculate_team_performance_vectors(matches_data: list) -> dict:
    """
    Calculate multidimensional performance vectors for each team.
    
    - Each team t has performance vector v_t = (goals_for, goals_against, points)
    - Performance metrics: scoring_rate, defensive_efficiency, points_per_match
    """
    team_stats = {}
    
    for match in matches_data:
        home_team = match['home_team']['home_team_name']
        away_team = match['away_team']['away_team_name']
        
        # Initialize team vectors
        for team in [home_team, away_team]:
            if team not in team_stats:
                team_stats[team] = {
                    'goals_for': 0, 'goals_against': 0, 
                    'points': 0, 'matches': 0
                }
        
        # Update performance vectors
        home_goals = match['home_score']
        away_goals = match['away_score']
        
        team_stats[home_team]['goals_for'] += home_goals
        team_stats[home_team]['goals_against'] += away_goals
        team_stats[away_team]['goals_for'] += away_goals
        team_stats[away_team]['goals_against'] += home_goals
        
        # Points allocation (3-1-0 system)
        if home_goals > away_goals:
            team_stats[home_team]['points'] += 3
        elif home_goals < away_goals:
            team_stats[away_team]['points'] += 3
        else:
            team_stats[home_team]['points'] += 1
            team_stats[away_team]['points'] += 1
        
        team_stats[home_team]['matches'] += 1
        team_stats[away_team]['matches'] += 1
    
    # Calculate derived metrics
    for team, stats in team_stats.items():
        if stats['matches'] > 0:
            stats['goals_per_match'] = stats['goals_for'] / stats['matches']
            stats['goals_conceded_per_match'] = stats['goals_against'] / stats['matches']
            stats['points_per_match'] = stats['points'] / stats['matches']
            stats['goal_difference'] = stats['goals_for'] - stats['goals_against']
    
    return team_stats

team_performance = calculate_team_performance_vectors(matches_data)

# Display top performers
sorted_teams = sorted(team_performance.items(), 
                     key=lambda x: x[1]['points_per_match'], reverse=True)

print("Top 5 Teams by Points Per Match:")
for i, (team, stats) in enumerate(sorted_teams[:5], 1):
    print(f"{i}. {team}: {stats['points_per_match']:.3f} PPM, "
          f"GD: {stats['goal_difference']:+d}")

Let T be the set of teams in the sample, and let matches be indexed by m = 1..n. Define a team performance vector for each team t in T:

where:

  • GF_t = total goals scored (“goals for”) across the sample
  • GA_t = total goals conceded (“goals against”) across the sample
  • P_t = total points under the 3–1–0 system
  • M_t = number of matches observed

Each match contributes an increment to the vector of each participating team. In other words, you are computing a set of sufficient summary statistics for the most basic season-level outcome model.

For a match between home team h and away team a with score (x, y):

  • home update:
    GF_h += x, GA_h += y, M_h += 1, and points P_h += {3,1,0} depending on sign(x - y)
  • away update:
    GF_a += y, GA_a += x, M_a += 1, and points P_a += {3,1,0} depending on sign(y - x)

So the full-season vector is just:

This is why the representation is stable and reproducible: it does not depend on arbitrary ordering or tuning parameters. It is a deterministic function of the match list.

Derived metrics are normalizations (rates). After building raw totals, you compute per-match rates:

  • scoring rate: GF_t / M_t (ourgoals_per_match)
  • conceding rate: GA_t / M_t (ourgoals_conceded_per_match)
  • efficiency under the points rule: P_t / M_t (ourpoints_per_match, abbreviated PPM)
  • goal difference: GD_t = GF_t - GA_t

Mathematically, this is a normalization map R^4 → R^4 that removes the scale effect of match count. Without the normalization, comparing teams is often meaningless when teams have different sample sizes.

3.2.3 Temporal dynamics and event sequences as stochastic processes

Let’s take a look at how events were distributed across a fixed match.

Let N(t) denote the cumulative number of recorded events up to minute t. The observed event rate is approximately 43.2 events/minute, placing the data in a high-frequency regime.

A mathematically clean baseline is a non-homogeneous Poisson process with intensity λ(t), where

Figure 3 indicates clear non-stationarity (spikes around structurally important moments such as half-time boundaries and stoppage), which motivates λ(t) as a function not only of clock time but also of match state (scoreline, substitutions, fatigue proxies). This is key.

Finally, we must understand that event data is an ordered object: a match is a time-indexed sequence of categorical states. Once you acknowledge that ordering, you’re immediately in the territory of stochastic processes.

Let the match event stream be the sequence:

where each e_i is an event type label (e.g., "Pass", "Carry", "Shot").

This function will approximate the event stream as a first-order Markov chain:

def analyze_event_sequences(events_df: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """
    Analyze mathematical properties of event sequences.
    
    Mathematical Framework:
    - Event sequence E forms a Markov chain with transition probabilities P(eᵢ₊₁|eᵢ)
    - We calculate transition matrices and sequence statistics
    """
    # Extract event type sequence
    event_sequence = events_df['type'].apply(
        lambda x: x['name'] if isinstance(x, dict) else str(x)
    ).tolist()
    
    # Calculate transition matrix
    unique_events = list(set(event_sequence))
    n_events = len(unique_events)
    transition_matrix = np.zeros((n_events, n_events))
    
    # Event type to index mapping
    event_to_idx = {event: i for i, event in enumerate(unique_events)}
    
    # Populate transition matrix
    for i in range(len(event_sequence) - 1):
        current_event = event_sequence[i]
        next_event = event_sequence[i + 1]
        
        curr_idx = event_to_idx[current_event]
        next_idx = event_to_idx[next_event]
        
        transition_matrix[curr_idx, next_idx] += 1
    
    # Normalize to probabilities
    row_sums = transition_matrix.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    transition_matrix = np.divide(transition_matrix, row_sums, 
                                 where=row_sums != 0, out=np.zeros_like(transition_matrix))
    
    # Calculate sequence properties
    sequence_length = len(event_sequence)
    unique_transitions = np.count_nonzero(transition_matrix)
    max_transitions = n_events * n_events
    
    print(f"EVENT SEQUENCE ANALYSIS:")
    print(f"  Sequence length: {sequence_length}")
    print(f"  State space size: {n_events}")
    print(f"  Observed transitions: {unique_transitions}/{max_transitions}")
    print(f"  Transition sparsity: {1 - unique_transitions/max_transitions:.3f}")
    
    return {
        'transition_matrix': transition_matrix,
        'event_mapping': event_to_idx,
        'sequence_stats': {
            'length': sequence_length,
            'states': n_events,
            'sparsity': 1 - unique_transitions/max_transitions
        }
    }

sequence_analysis = analyze_event_sequences(events_df)

Recall the Markov assumption says:

But this is not claiming football has no memory. It’s saying: as a baseline, compress history into the current event type and measure what tends to follow what. This is valuable because it converts a messy sequence into a concrete object you can compute and reason about: a transition matrix. This is one of my favorite models.

3.3 Why this is important

Overall, the hierarchical data structure and properties identified in this section establish the foundation for the subsequent advanced analytical techniques we will talk about in the next few sections:

Network Science (Section 6): Event sequences and player interactions form complex networks suitable for graph-theoretic analysis using centrality measures and community detection.

Bayesian Inference (Section 8): Small sample sizes and prior knowledge requirements necessitate Bayesian approaches for performance estimation and uncertainty quantification.

Spatial Modeling (Section 9): Bounded coordinate system and spatial dependencies allow for advanced spatial statistical modeling and territory control analysis.

Machine Learning (Section 10): High-dimensional event data with categorical and continuous features provides rich substrate for supervised and unsupervised learning applications.

4. Event Data Structure

When we examine event data in detail, we discover that football can be decomposed into eight primary categories of actions, each representing different aspects of the game’s flow and dynamics.

— Ball Movement dominates the event landscape, accounting for approximately 80.8% of all recorded events. This category encompasses passes, carries, and ball receipts — the fundamental actions that drive possession-based football. The sheer volume of ball movement events reflects football’s essence as a possession game, where teams spend the majority of their time attempting to maintain, advance, or regain control of the ball.

— Set Pieces represent the second most frequent category at 7.2% of events. This includes free kicks, corners, throw-ins, and kick-offs. While less frequent than ball movement, set pieces carry disproportionate strategic importance, often representing the highest-probability scoring opportunities outside of open play.

— Defensive Actions comprise 4.7% of events and include tackles, interceptions, blocks, and clearances. These events represent the reactive side of football, where teams attempt to disrupt their opponents’ attacking intentions. The relatively lower frequency masks their critical importance in determining possession transitions and defensive solidity.

To categorize in a subsequence of events:

# Loading and analyzing event structure
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter

# Load event data for comprehensive analysis
events_df = pd.read_json(r'C:\Users\Lucas\Documents\Research\Datasets\StatsBombOpenData\data\events\15946.json')

print(f"Total events analyzed: {len(events_df):,}")
print(f"Event types identified: {events_df['type'].nunique()}")
print(f"Time span covered: {events_df['minute'].min()}-{events_df['minute'].max()} minutes")

# Categorize events into meaningful groups
event_categories = {
    'Ball Movement': ['Pass', 'Ball Receipt*', 'Carry'],
    'Attacking Actions': ['Shot', 'Dribble', 'Offensive Foul'],
    'Defensive Actions': ['Tackle', 'Interception', 'Block', 'Clearance', 'Aerial Won'],
    'Set Pieces': ['Free Kick', 'Corner Kick', 'Throw-in', 'Kick Off', 'Goal Kick'],
    'Goalkeeper Actions': ['Goalkeeper', 'Save'],
    'Fouls & Cards': ['Foul Committed', 'Yellow Card', 'Red Card'],
    'Game Management': ['Substitution', 'Injury', 'Referee Event'],
    'Miscellaneous': ['Dispossessed', 'Error', 'Miscontrol', 'Bad Behaviour']
}

The spatial dimension of event data reveals some really fascinating patterns about how football utilizes the pitch.

The pitch is naturally divided into zones that reflect tactical understanding: defensive thirds, middle thirds, and attacking thirds. However, the raw coordinate data allows for much more granular analysis. Events cluster heavily in central areas, reflecting the natural flow of play through midfield channels, while the extreme wide areas and corners show lower event density.

# Analyze spatial distribution patterns
events_with_location = events_df.dropna(subset=['location'])
total_events_spatial = len(events_with_location)
spatial_coverage = (total_events_spatial / len(events_df)) * 100

print(f"Spatial coverage: {spatial_coverage:.1f}%")

# Extract coordinates and analyze field zones
locations = pd.DataFrame(events_with_location['location'].tolist(), columns=['x', 'y'])
locations['zone_x'] = pd.cut(locations['x'], bins=[0, 40, 80, 120], labels=['Defensive', 'Middle', 'Attacking'])
locations['zone_y'] = pd.cut(locations['y'], bins=[0, 27, 53, 80], labels=['Left', 'Center', 'Right'])

zone_distribution = locations.groupby(['zone_x', 'zone_y']).size().reset_index(name='event_count')
zone_distribution['percentage'] = (zone_distribution['event_count'] / len(locations)) * 100

The temporal dimension reveals how football matches evolve over time. Event frequency doesn’t remain constant throughout the 90-minute duration — instead, it follows predictable patterns that reflect the natural rhythms of the sport.

The opening 45 minutes typically show higher event density as teams begin with full energy and tactical clarity. Event rates often peak in the 10–20 minute range as teams settle into their tactical approaches. The break between halves creates a natural discontinuity in event patterns. Teams often emerge from half-time with tactical adjustments that can be detected through changes in event types and spatial distributions. The last 15 minutes of matches often show increased event frequency, particularly in categories related to attacking actions and set pieces. This reflects the psychological pressure of approaching full-time and the tactical urgency to influence the result. And added time periods show distinctly different event profiles, with higher frequencies of defensive actions, fouls, and time-wasting behaviors as teams attempt to manage game state.

# Analyze temporal patterns
events_df['minute_bin'] = pd.cut(events_df['minute'], 
                                bins=range(0, 105, 15), 
                                labels=['0-15', '15-30', '30-45', '45-60', '60-75', '75-90', '90+'])

temporal_analysis = events_df.groupby('minute_bin').agg({
    'type': 'count',
    'team': lambda x: len(x.unique()),
    'possession_team': lambda x: x.mode().iloc[0] if not x.empty else None
}).reset_index()

temporal_analysis.columns = ['Time_Period', 'Event_Count', 'Active_Teams', 'Dominant_Possession_Team']
temporal_analysis['Events_Per_Minute'] = temporal_analysis['Event_Count'] / 15

5. Visualizations with MPL Soccer

The journey from raw event data to meaningful visual analysis represents one of the most crucial steps in football analytics. While pandas and matplotlib provide the foundation for data manipulation and basic plotting, the specialized demands of football visualization require tools designed specifically for the sport. This is where MPL Soccer emerges as a very key library.

Get Lucas Carrasquilla’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Traditional data visualization approaches, like the ones seen in the previous sections, while mathematically sound, often fail to capture the spatial and contextual richness that defines football. A scatter plot of shot locations might show where attempts occurred, but it lacks the geographical context that makes football analysis meaningful. The pitch itself becomes a crucial frame of reference, understanding whether a shot came from the penalty area versus the center circle fundamentally changes its significance. MPL Soccer addresses this challenge by providing a framework built specifically for football data visualization. Developed by Andrew Rowlinson, the library emerged from the recognition that football analytics required specialized tools that could handle the unique coordinate system of a football pitch.

5.1 Basics of MPL Soccer’s architecture

At its core, this library extends matplotlib’s capabilities by providing specialized classes and methods designed for football-specific visualizations.

The Pitchclass serves as the foundational element, providing multiple pitch types that correspond to different data providers and coordinate systems. StatsBomb’s coordinate system, which uses a 120x80 unit pitch with the origin at one corner, requires different handling than other providers who might use percentage-based coordinates or center-origin systems. MPL Soccer abstracts these differences, allowing analysts to work with their preferred data source without worrying about coordinate transformations.

Let’s instantiate a Pitch object:

from mplsoccer import Pitch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# Create the pitch visualization
pitch = Pitch(pitch_type='statsbomb', pitch_color='#2e5e3e', 
              line_color='white', linewidth=2)
fig, ax = pitch.draw(figsize=(16, 11))

The pitch is now ready for event plotting with our coordinate system.

5.2 Passing networks

To create a basic passing network visualization:

# Extract pass data
def get_event_type(event):
    if isinstance(event.get('type'), dict):
        return event['type'].get('name', 'Unknown')
    return str(event.get('type', 'Unknown'))

# Filter for passes
passes_df = events_df[events_df['event_type'] == 'Pass']

# Plot pass connections
for idx, pass_event in passes_df.iterrows():
    if (pass_event.get('location') is not None and 
        pass_event['pass'].get('end_location') is not None):
        start_x, start_y = pass_event['location']
        end_x, end_y = pass_event['pass']['end_location']
        
        ax.annotate('', xy=(end_x, end_y), xytext=(start_x, start_y),
                   arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='yellow', 
                                 alpha=0.7, lw=2))

You can do this at the player level, like in this example, to see how a given player’s passing affected the game. However, a more useful technique is to plot players’ median positions during a match and the players they passed to. We typically draw circles for players and arrows for passes, with arrow thickness indicating how frequently each pass was played.

Here’s an example:

import pandas as pd
  import numpy as np
  import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
  from mplsoccer import Pitch
  from collections import defaultdict

  # Load and clean StatsBomb data
  events_df = pd.read_json('path_to_events.json')

  # Helper function to extract names from nested dictionaries
  def extract_name(obj):
      if isinstance(obj, dict):
          return obj.get('name', 'Unknown')
      return str(obj)

  # Clean up data structure
  events_df['team_name'] = events_df['team'].apply(extract_name)
  events_df['player_name'] = events_df['player'].apply(lambda x: extract_name(x) if x is not None else None)
  events_df['event_type'] = events_df['type'].apply(extract_name)

  # Filter team data
  team_name = events_df['team_name'].iloc[0]
  team_events = events_df[events_df['team_name'] == team_name]
  passes_df = team_events[team_events['event_type'] == 'Pass']

  # Calculate average positions
  player_positions = defaultdict(list)
  for idx, event in team_events.iterrows():
      player = event.get('player_name')
      location = event.get('location')
      if player and location and isinstance(location, list) and len(location) == 2:
          player_positions[player].append(location)

  # Get average positions for active players
  avg_positions = {}
  for player, positions in player_positions.items():
      if len(positions) >= 15:
          positions_array = np.array(positions)
          avg_x = np.mean(positions_array[:, 0])
          avg_y = np.mean(positions_array[:, 1])
          avg_positions[player] = (avg_x, avg_y)

  # Calculate pass connections
  pass_connections = defaultdict(int)
  for idx, pass_event in passes_df.iterrows():
      passer = pass_event.get('player_name')
      pass_info = pass_event.get('pass')

      if isinstance(pass_info, dict):
          recipient_info = pass_info.get('recipient')
          receiver = extract_name(recipient_info) if recipient_info else None

          # Check if pass was successful
          pass_outcome = pass_info.get('outcome')
          is_successful = not (isinstance(pass_outcome, dict) and pass_outcome.get('name') == 'Incomplete')

          if (passer and receiver and is_successful and
              passer in avg_positions and receiver in avg_positions):
              pass_connections[(passer, receiver)] += 1

  # Create visualization
  fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 11))
  pitch = Pitch(pitch_type='statsbomb', pitch_color='#2d5a2d', line_color='white', linewidth=3)
  pitch.draw(ax=ax)

  # Filter significant connections
  min_passes = 5
  significant_connections = {k: v for k, v in pass_connections.items() if v >= min_passes}
  max_passes = max(significant_connections.values()) if significant_connections else 1

  # Draw pass connections with thickness based on frequency
  for (passer, receiver), count in significant_connections.items():
      passer_pos = avg_positions[passer]
      receiver_pos = avg_positions[receiver]

      line_thickness = 1 + (count / max_passes) * 11
      alpha = 0.3 + (count / max_passes) * 0.6

      ax.plot([passer_pos[0], receiver_pos[0]], [passer_pos[1], receiver_pos[1]],
             color='white', linewidth=line_thickness, alpha=alpha, zorder=2)

  # Draw player nodes (top 11 most active)
  top_players = sorted(avg_positions.items(),
                      key=lambda x: len(player_positions[x[0]]), reverse=True)[:11]

  for i, (player, (x, y)) in enumerate(top_players):
      circle = plt.Circle((x, y), radius=3.5, color='#FF4444',
                         edgecolor='white', linewidth=3, zorder=5)
      ax.add_patch(circle)

      # Position abbreviation based on field coordinates
      position_abbr = get_position_abbrev(x, y)  # Custom function for position naming
      ax.text(x, y, position_abbr, color='white', fontweight='bold',
             ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11, zorder=6)
